To fix (3)

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 4107 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 8 codebook/README/label sources and 4107 data columns across 134 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To fix Repository Check

What we found

  • We could not check 1 repository: https://osf.io/q3wzh (closed registration source).
  • We found 282 files in 2 repositories.
  • We found 7 README files and 0 repositories without READMEs.
  • We found 1 registration-linked OSF project that is closed with no files reachable anywhere.
  • The manuscript’s studies and the repository’s file groups do not match.
  • We found 84 files with a naming suggestion.
  • We left out 17 files that do not belong in a repository: compiled Python files (10), operating system (7). Remove them from the repository.

Registration Points to a Closed Project

1 OSF project (https://osf.io/q3wzh) is referenced by a registration in this manuscript, but it is closed or inaccessible, and no copy of its files could be found anywhere else. Some OSF registrations only describe what was shared, while the actual files live in the project they were registered from — if that project is closed and the registration holds no copy, metacheck cannot list or download its files, and other researchers cannot access them either. Consider making the source project openly available, or re-uploading its files directly into the registration.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (ex4) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 17 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: compiled Python files (10), operating system (7). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 13 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 4107 columns across 134 data files.

Issues Identified

74 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

537 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 529 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 4 of 134 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 9 R code files.

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

File paths

2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: factor_loadings_summary.csv to factor_analysis/results_r/factor_loadings_summary.csv (in export_factor_loadings_v2.R); /Users/mhhuang/Psychometrics4AI_revision/multi_model_studies to . (in run_explicit_all_combinations.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 2 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: study1_with_simulation_result.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 4 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 3 scripts need a person to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: cfa_analysis_simple.R, multi_model_studies/correlation_significance_test/study_2_binary_score/correlation_significance_test.R, multi_model_studies/correlation_significance_test/study_3_binary_score/correlation_significance_test.R. Naming the file in the script solves this.

> build_cfa_model_for <- function(domains, present_cols) {
>   lines <- c()
>   for (lat in names(domains)) {
>     items_present <- intersect(domains[[lat]], present_cols)
>     if (length(items_present) >= 2) {  # be permissive; std.lv=TRUE helps identification
>       rhs <- paste(items_present, collapse = " + ")
>       lines <- c(lines, sprintf("%s =~ %s", lat, rhs))
>     }
>   }
>   if (length(lines) == 0) return(NULL)
>   paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
> }
> sanitize <- function(x) {
>   x %>% tolower() %>%
>     str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9]+", "_") %>%
>     str_replace_all("^_|_$", "")
> }
> parse_meta <- function(filepath) {
>   # Extract both filename and path parts
>   filename <- basename(filepath)
>   path_parts <- strsplit(filepath, "/")[[1]]
> 
>   # Extract study from path structure (similar to cfa_analysis_simple.R logic)
>   study <- case_when(
>     any(grepl("study_2a", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "STUDY_2",
>     any(grepl("study_2b", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "STUDY_3",
>     # Fallback to filename-based detection
>     str_detect(filename, regex("study[_-]?2", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "STUDY_2",
>     str_detect(filename, regex("study[_-]?3", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "STUDY_3",
>     TRUE ~ "UNKNOWN"
>   )
> 
>   # Determine condition from path structure (similar to run_batch_r_analysis.sh logic)
>   condition <- case_when(
>     any(grepl("binary.*simple|simple.*binary", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "Simple Binary",
>     any(grepl("binary.*elaborated|elaborated.*binary", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "Elaborated Binary",
>     any(grepl("expanded", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "Expanded Format",
>     any(grepl("likert", path_parts, ignore.case = TRUE)) ~ "Likert",
>     # Fallback to filename-based detection
>     str_detect(filename, regex("binary[_-]?simple|simple[_-]?binary", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Simple Binary",
>     str_detect(filename, regex("binary[_-]?elaborated|elaborated[_-]?binary", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Elaborated Binary",
>     str_detect(filename, regex("expanded|expanded[_-]?format|expformat", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Expanded Format",
>     str_detect(filename, regex("likert", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Likert",
>     str_detect(filename, regex("\\bbinary\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Binary",
>     TRUE ~ "Unknown"
>   )
> 
>   # Extract model from filename with improved patterns
>   model_patterns <- c("openai[-_]?gpt[-_]?3[.]?5[-_]?turbo", "gpt[-_]?3[.]?5[-_]?turbo",
>                       "gpt[-_]?4o", "gpt[-_]?4", "llama", "deepseek",
>                       "claude", "gemini", "mistral", "qwen", "phi", "o1", "o3")
>   model <- "unknown"
>   for (pat in model_patterns) {
>     if (str_detect(filename, regex(pat, ignore_case = TRUE))) {
>       extracted <- str_extract(filename, regex(pat, ignore_case = TRUE))
>       # Clean up common variations
>       model <- case_when(
>         str_detect(extracted, regex("(openai.*)?gpt.*3.*5", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "gpt_3.5",
>         str_detect(extracted, regex("gpt.*4o", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "gpt_4o",
>         str_detect(extracted, regex("gpt.*4", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "gpt_4",
>         TRUE ~ str_replace_all(tolower(extracted), "[-.]", "_")
>       )
>       break
>     }
>   }
> 
>   list(study = study, condition = condition, model = model)
> }

> correlations$Avg <- rowMeans(correlations[, c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N")], na.rm = TRUE)
> human_correlations <- c(O = 0.7504, C = 0.8399, E = 0.8846, A = 0.7962, N = 0.7385)
> human_avg <- mean(human_correlations)
> n1 <- 438
> n2 <- 438
> domains <- c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N", "Avg")
> results_list <- list()
> all_p_values <- c()
> perform_test <- function(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model) {
>   # Check for valid correlations (must be between -1 and 1, not equal to 1 or -1)
>   if (is.na(ai_corr) || is.na(human_corr) || 
>       abs(ai_corr) >= 1 || abs(human_corr) >= 1) {
>     return(list(
>       condition = condition,
>       model = model,
>       domain = domain,
>       ai_corr = ai_corr,
>       human_corr = human_corr,
>       statistic = NA,
>       p_value = NA,
>       significant = FALSE
>     ))
>   }
>   
>   # Fisher's z-transformation for both correlations
>   z_ai <- 0.5 * log((1 + ai_corr) / (1 - ai_corr))
>   z_human <- 0.5 * log((1 + human_corr) / (1 - human_corr))
>   
>   # Standard error for the difference (assuming independent samples)
>   se_diff <- sqrt((1/(n1-3)) + (1/(n2-3)))
>   
>   # Test statistic
>   z_stat <- (z_ai - z_human) / se_diff
>   
>   # Two-sided p-value
>   p_value <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))
>   
>   return(list(
>     condition = condition,
>     model = model,
>     domain = domain,
>     ai_corr = ai_corr,
>     human_corr = human_corr,
>     statistic = z_stat,
>     p_value = p_value,
>     significant = p_value < 0.05
>   ))
> }
> for(i in 1:nrow(correlations)) {
>   condition <- correlations$Condition[i]
>   model <- correlations$Model[i]
>   
>   for(domain in domains) {
>     if(domain == "Avg") {
>       ai_corr <- correlations$Avg[i]
>       human_corr <- human_avg
>     } else {
>       ai_corr <- correlations[[domain]][i]
>       human_corr <- human_correlations[domain]
>     }
>     
>     result <- perform_test(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model)
>     results_list <- append(results_list, list(result))
>     all_p_values <- c(all_p_values, result$p_value)
>   }
> }
> results_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results_list, function(x) {
>   # Handle NA values safely
>   data.frame(
>     Condition = ifelse(is.null(x$condition) || is.na(x$condition), "Unknown", x$condition),
>     Model = ifelse(is.null(x$model) || is.na(x$model), "Unknown", x$model),
>     Domain = ifelse(is.null(x$domain) || is.na(x$domain), "Unknown", x$domain),
>     AI_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr), NA, round(x$ai_corr, 4)),
>     Human_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr), NA, round(x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Difference = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr) || is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr), 
>                         NA, round(x$ai_corr - x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Test_Statistic = ifelse(is.null(x$statistic) || is.na(x$statistic), NA, round(x$statistic, 4)),
>     P_Value = ifelse(is.null(x$p_value) || is.na(x$p_value), NA, round(x$p_value, 6)),
>     Significant = ifelse(is.null(x$significant) || is.na(x$significant), FALSE, x$significant),
>     Bonferroni_P_Global = NA,  # Global correction (all 120 tests)
>     Bonferroni_Significant_Global = FALSE,
>     Bonferroni_P_Domain = NA,  # Domain-wise correction (20 tests per domain)
>     Bonferroni_Significant_Domain = FALSE,
>     stringsAsFactors = FALSE
>   )
> }))
> rownames(results_df) <- 1:nrow(results_df)

> if(length(valid_p_values) > 0) {

>   bonferroni_alpha_global <- 0.05 / n_tests_global
>   bonferroni_p_values_global <- p.adjust(valid_p_values, method = "bonferroni")
>   
>   # Fill in Global Bonferroni results for valid tests
>   results_df$Bonferroni_P_Global[valid_p_indices] <- round(bonferroni_p_values_global, 6)
>   results_df$Bonferroni_Significant_Global[valid_p_indices] <- bonferroni_p_values_global < 0.05
> } else {
>   n_tests_global <- 0
>   bonferroni_alpha_global <- NA

> normalize_model <- function(x) {
>   x <- str_trim(x)
>   dplyr::case_when(
>     x %in% c("openai_gpt_3.5_turbo_0125", "gpt-3.5", "gpt_3.5") ~ "gpt-3.5",
>     x %in% c("gpt_4", "gpt-4")                                   ~ "gpt-4",
>     x %in% c("gpt_4o", "gpt-4o", "openai_gpt_4o")                ~ "gpt-4o",
>     x %in% c("llama", "meta_llama")                              ~ "llama",
>     x %in% c("deepseek")                                         ~ "deepseek",
>     TRUE ~ x
>   )
> }
> normalize_condition <- function(x) {
>   x0 <- str_squish(str_trim(x))
>   # lower for matching, but return canonical title-cased strings
>   xl <- tolower(x0)
>   dplyr::case_when(
>     xl %in% c("simple binary", "binary", "simple-binary") ~ "Simple Binary",
>     xl %in% c("elaborated binary", "elaborated-binary")   ~ "Elaborated Binary",
>     xl %in% c("expanded format", "expanded-format")       ~ "Expanded Format",
>     
>     # Likert variants commonly seen
>     xl %in% c("likert format", "likert", "bfi-2 likert", "bfi-2-likert",
>               "bfi2 likert", "bfi2-likert", "bfi-2 likert format",
>               "bfi-2-likert-format", "bfi2 likert format", "bfi2-likert-format") ~ "Likert Format",
>     
>     TRUE ~ x0  # leave as-is if it already matches
>   )
> }
> condition_levels <- c("Simple Binary", "Elaborated Binary", "Expanded Format", "Likert Format")
> model_levels     <- c("gpt-3.5", "gpt-4", "gpt-4o", "llama", "deepseek")
> raw <- read_csv(csv_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
> required_cols <- c(

> missing_cols <- setdiff(required_cols, colnames(raw))

>     N = bfi_sim_N
>   ) %>%
>   arrange(Condition, Model) %>%

> human_correlations <- c(O = 0.7504, C = 0.8399, E = 0.8846, A = 0.7962, N = 0.7385)
> human_avg <- mean(human_correlations)
> n1 <- 438
> n2 <- 438
> domains <- c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N", "Avg")
> results_list <- list()
> perform_test <- function(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model) {
>   if (is.na(ai_corr) || is.na(human_corr) ||
>       abs(ai_corr) >= 1 || abs(human_corr) >= 1) {
>     return(list(
>       condition = condition,
>       model = model,
>       domain = domain,
>       ai_corr = ai_corr,
>       human_corr = human_corr,
>       statistic = NA_real_,
>       p_value = NA_real_,
>       significant = FALSE
>     ))
>   }
>   z_ai <- 0.5 * log((1 + ai_corr) / (1 - ai_corr))
>   z_human <- 0.5 * log((1 + human_corr) / (1 - human_corr))
>   se_diff <- sqrt((1/(n1 - 3)) + (1/(n2 - 3)))
>   z_stat <- (z_ai - z_human) / se_diff
>   p_value <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))
>   
>   list(
>     condition = condition,
>     model = model,
>     domain = domain,
>     ai_corr = ai_corr,
>     human_corr = human_corr,
>     statistic = z_stat,
>     p_value = p_value,
>     significant = is.finite(p_value) && (p_value < 0.05)
>   )
> }
> for (i in 1:nrow(correlations)) {
>   condition <- as.character(correlations$Condition[i])
>   model     <- as.character(correlations$Model[i])
>   
>   for (domain in domains) {
>     if (domain == "Avg") {
>       ai_corr    <- correlations$Avg[i]
>       human_corr <- human_avg
>     } else {
>       ai_corr    <- correlations[[domain]][i]
>       human_corr <- human_correlations[[domain]]
>     }
>     results_list <- append(results_list, list(
>       perform_test(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model)
>     ))
>   }
> }
> results_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results_list, function(x) {

> correlations$Avg <- rowMeans(correlations[, c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N")], na.rm = TRUE)
> human_correlations <- c(O = 0.7504, C = 0.8399, E = 0.8846, A = 0.7962, N = 0.7385)
> human_avg <- mean(human_correlations)
> n1 <- 200
> n2 <- 438
> domains <- c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N", "Avg")
> results_list <- list()
> all_p_values <- c()
> perform_test <- function(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model) {
>   # Check for valid correlations (must be between -1 and 1, not equal to 1 or -1)
>   if (is.na(ai_corr) || is.na(human_corr) || 
>       abs(ai_corr) >= 1 || abs(human_corr) >= 1) {
>     return(list(
>       condition = condition,
>       model = model,
>       domain = domain,
>       ai_corr = ai_corr,
>       human_corr = human_corr,
>       statistic = NA,
>       p_value = NA,
>       significant = FALSE
>     ))
>   }
>   
>   # Fisher's z-transformation for both correlations
>   z_ai <- 0.5 * log((1 + ai_corr) / (1 - ai_corr))
>   z_human <- 0.5 * log((1 + human_corr) / (1 - human_corr))
>   
>   # Standard error for the difference (assuming independent samples)
>   se_diff <- sqrt((1/(n1-3)) + (1/(n2-3)))
>   
>   # Test statistic
>   z_stat <- (z_ai - z_human) / se_diff
>   
>   # Two-sided p-value
>   p_value <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))
>   
>   return(list(
>     condition = condition,
>     model = model,
>     domain = domain,
>     ai_corr = ai_corr,
>     human_corr = human_corr,
>     statistic = z_stat,
>     p_value = p_value,
>     significant = p_value < 0.05
>   ))
> }
> for(i in 1:nrow(correlations)) {
>   condition <- correlations$Condition[i]
>   model <- correlations$Model[i]
>   
>   for(domain in domains) {
>     if(domain == "Avg") {
>       ai_corr <- correlations$Avg[i]
>       human_corr <- human_avg
>     } else {
>       ai_corr <- correlations[[domain]][i]
>       human_corr <- human_correlations[domain]
>     }
>     
>     result <- perform_test(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, condition, model)
>     results_list <- append(results_list, list(result))
>     all_p_values <- c(all_p_values, result$p_value)
>   }
> }
> results_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results_list, function(x) {
>   # Handle NA values safely
>   data.frame(
>     Condition = ifelse(is.null(x$condition) || is.na(x$condition), "Unknown", x$condition),
>     Model = ifelse(is.null(x$model) || is.na(x$model), "Unknown", x$model),
>     Domain = ifelse(is.null(x$domain) || is.na(x$domain), "Unknown", x$domain),
>     AI_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr), NA, round(x$ai_corr, 4)),
>     Human_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr), NA, round(x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Difference = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr) || is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr), 
>                         NA, round(x$ai_corr - x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Test_Statistic = ifelse(is.null(x$statistic) || is.na(x$statistic), NA, round(x$statistic, 4)),
>     P_Value = ifelse(is.null(x$p_value) || is.na(x$p_value), NA, round(x$p_value, 6)),
>     Significant = ifelse(is.null(x$significant) || is.na(x$significant), FALSE, x$significant),

>   )
> }))

> condition_levels <- c("Simple Binary", "Elaborated Binary", "Expanded Format", "Likert Format")
> model_levels     <- c("gpt-3.5", "gpt-4", "gpt-4o", "llama", "deepseek")
> raw <- read_csv(csv_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
> required_cols <- c(
>   "format", "model",
>   "O_correlation", "C_correlation", "E_correlation", "A_correlation", "N_correlation"
> )
> missing_cols <- setdiff(required_cols, colnames(raw))
> if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
>   stop(sprintf("Missing columns in CSV: %s", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")))
> }
> tmp <- raw %>%
>   mutate(
>     Condition_chr = normalize_condition(format),
>     Model_chr     = normalize_model(model)
>   )
> unknown_conditions <- setdiff(unique(tmp$Condition_chr), condition_levels)
> if (length(unknown_conditions) > 0) {
>   warning(sprintf(
>     "Found format values not in expected set; leaving as-is: %s",
>     paste(unknown_conditions, collapse = ", ")
>   ))
> }
> correlations <- tmp %>%
>   transmute(
>     format = factor(Condition_chr, levels = condition_levels),
>     Model     = factor(Model_chr,     levels = model_levels),
>     O = O_correlation,
>     C = C_correlation,
>     E = E_correlation,
>     A = A_correlation,
>     N = N_correlation
>   ) %>%
>   arrange(format, Model) %>%
>   as.data.frame()
> correlations$Avg <- rowMeans(correlations[, c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N")], na.rm = TRUE)
> human_correlations <- c(O = 0.7504, C = 0.8399, E = 0.8846, A = 0.7962, N = 0.7385)
> human_avg <- mean(human_correlations)
> n1 <- 200
> n2 <- 438
> domains <- c("O", "C", "E", "A", "N", "Avg")
> results_list <- list()
> perform_test <- function(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, format, model) {
>   if (is.na(ai_corr) || is.na(human_corr) ||
>       abs(ai_corr) >= 1 || abs(human_corr) >= 1) {
>     return(list(
>       format = format,
>       model = model,
>       domain = domain,
>       ai_corr = ai_corr,
>       human_corr = human_corr,
>       statistic = NA_real_,
>       p_value = NA_real_,
>       significant = FALSE
>     ))
>   }
>   z_ai <- 0.5 * log((1 + ai_corr) / (1 - ai_corr))
>   z_human <- 0.5 * log((1 + human_corr) / (1 - human_corr))
>   se_diff <- sqrt((1/(n1 - 3)) + (1/(n2 - 3)))
>   z_stat <- (z_ai - z_human) / se_diff
>   p_value <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))
>   
>   list(
>     format = format,
>     model = model,
>     domain = domain,
>     ai_corr = ai_corr,
>     human_corr = human_corr,
>     statistic = z_stat,
>     p_value = p_value,
>     significant = is.finite(p_value) && (p_value < 0.05)
>   )
> }
> for (i in 1:nrow(correlations)) {
>   format <- as.character(correlations$format[i])
>   model     <- as.character(correlations$Model[i])
>   
>   for (domain in domains) {
>     if (domain == "Avg") {
>       ai_corr    <- correlations$Avg[i]
>       human_corr <- human_avg
>     } else {
>       ai_corr    <- correlations[[domain]][i]
>       human_corr <- human_correlations[[domain]]
>     }
>     results_list <- append(results_list, list(
>       perform_test(ai_corr, human_corr, domain, format, model)
>     ))
>   }
> }
> results_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results_list, function(x) {
>   data.frame(
>     format = ifelse(is.null(x$format) || is.na(x$format), "Unknown", x$format),
>     Model = ifelse(is.null(x$model) || is.na(x$model), "Unknown", x$model),
>     Domain = ifelse(is.null(x$domain) || is.na(x$domain), "Unknown", x$domain),
>     AI_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr), NA, round(x$ai_corr, 4)),
>     Human_Correlation = ifelse(is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr), NA, round(x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Difference = ifelse(is.null(x$ai_corr) || is.na(x$ai_corr) || is.null(x$human_corr) || is.na(x$human_corr),
>                         NA, round(x$ai_corr - x$human_corr, 4)),
>     Test_Statistic = ifelse(is.null(x$statistic) || is.na(x$statistic), NA, round(x$statistic, 4)),
>     P_Value = ifelse(is.null(x$p_value) || is.na(x$p_value), NA, round(x$p_value, 6)),
>     Significant = ifelse(is.null(x$significant) || is.na(x$significant), FALSE, x$significant),
>     Bonferroni_P_Global = NA_real_,
>     Bonferroni_Significant_Global = FALSE,
>     Bonferroni_P_Domain = NA_real_,
>     Bonferroni_Significant_Domain = FALSE,
>     stringsAsFactors = FALSE
>   )
> }))
> rownames(results_df) <- 1:nrow(results_df)
> valid_p_indices <- !is.na(results_df$P_Value)
> valid_p_values  <- results_df$P_Value[valid_p_indices]
> if (length(valid_p_values) > 0) {
>   n_tests_global <- length(valid_p_values)
>   bonferroni_alpha_global <- 0.05 / n_tests_global
>   bonferroni_p_values_global <- p.adjust(valid_p_values, method = "bonferroni")
>   
>   results_df$Bonferroni_P_Global[valid_p_indices] <- round(bonferroni_p_values_global, 6)
>   results_df$Bonferroni_Significant_Global[valid_p_indices] <- bonferroni_p_values_global < 0.05
> } else {
>   n_tests_global <- 0
>   bonferroni_alpha_global <- NA_real_
> }
> for (domain in domains) {
>   domain_indices <- results_df$Domain == domain & !is.na(results_df$P_Value)
>   domain_p_values <- results_df$P_Value[domain_indices]
>   
>   if (length(domain_p_values) > 0) {
>     n_tests_domain <- length(domain_p_values)
>     bonferroni_alpha_domain <- 0.05 / n_tests_domain
>     bonferroni_p_values_domain <- p.adjust(domain_p_values, method = "bonferroni")
>     
>     results_df$Bonferroni_P_Domain[domain_indices] <- round(bonferroni_p_values_domain, 6)
>     results_df$Bonferroni_Significant_Domain[domain_indices] <- bonferroni_p_values_domain < 0.05
>     
>     cat(sprintf("Domain %s: %d tests, corrected alpha = %.6f\n",
>                 domain, n_tests_domain, bonferroni_alpha_domain))
>   }
> }

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 33 Python code files.

Run order

A dependency cycle was detected among 2 files (study_3_binary_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_3_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 33 scripts: 8 ran without error, 19 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 6 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: mini_marker_prompt.py (by simulation_utils.py, multi_model_studies/study_2a/recover_missing_participants.py, study_2_binary_baseline_simulation.ipynb, study_2_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_2_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, multi_model_studies/study_2b/recover_missing_participants.py, study_3_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_3_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb); moral_stories.py (by simulation_utils.py, multi_model_studies/study_3/recover_missing_participants.py, study_3_generalized_combined_simulation.py, study_3_generalized_moral_simulation.py, study_3_moral_multi_model_simulation.py); risk_taking.py (by simulation_utils.py, multi_model_studies/study_3/recover_missing_participants.py, study_3_generalized_combined_simulation.py, study_3_generalized_risk_simulation.py, study_3_risk_multi_model_simulation.py); schema_bfi2.py (by study_2_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_2_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, multi_model_studies/study_2b/recover_missing_participants.py, study_3_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_3_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb); schema_tda.py (by binary_baseline_prompt.py, mini_marker_prompt.py); simulation_utils.py (by multi_model_studies/study_2a/recover_missing_participants.py, study_2_binary_baseline_simulation.ipynb, study_2_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_2_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, multi_model_studies/study_2b/recover_missing_participants.py, study_3_binary_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_3_expanded_multi_model_simulation.ipynb, study_3_likert_multi_model_simulation.ipynb). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

=== Binary Baseline Prompt ===
### Your Assigned Personality ### 
Based on your personality profile below, please rate yourself on the following traits.
You are high in Extraversion. You are outgoing, sociable, assertive, and energetic. You are low in Agreeableness. You tend to be skeptical, competitive, and direct in your interactions. You are high in Conscientiousness. You are organized, responsible, hardworking, and reliable. You are low in Neuroticism. You are emotionally stable, calm, and resilient under stress. You are high in Openness. You are curious, creative, open to new experiences, and intellectually engaged.

### Context and Objective ###
You are participating in a study to help us understand human personality.

Your job is to fill out a personality questionnaire below. Your questionnaire answers should be reflective of your assigned personalities.

### Response Format ###
IMPORTANT: You must provide ratings for ALL 40 traits listed below.
Return ONLY a JSON object where:
- Keys are the exact trait names (e.g., "Bashful", "Bold", etc.)
- Values are numbers from 1-9 based on the rating scale
- Include ALL 40 traits - no more, no less
- Do NOT include personality domains like "Extraversion" or "Agreeableness"
- Do NOT add any text outside the JSON

Example format:
{
    "Bashful": 7,
    "Bold": 3,
    "Careless": 2,
    ...
    "Withdrawn": 4
}

Dependencies were installed into a throwaway library before running (pip install): 14 succeeded, 0 failed. anthropic, azure, google, matplotlib, numpy, openai, pandas, python-dotenv, requests, scikit-learn, scipy, seaborn, statsmodels, tenacity were installed.

All code and output

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

9 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 80 result tables (462 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

Where the files sit within each repository. Each file is followed by how it was classified, which study it belongs to; junk files, hidden files and empty folders are marked.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

template_name OSF Preregistration
title Examining the Association between Big Five Personality Traits and Decision-Making Tendency
id 4t9bf
link https://osf.io/4t9bf
date_created 2024-09-08T07:32:32.715267
date_modified 2024-09-08T07:32:32.553505
date_registered 2024-09-08T07:32:32.682264
embargo_end_date
ia_url https://archive.org/details/osf-registrations-4t9bf-v1
research_questions 1. Big Five Personality traits are linked to people’s risk taking tendency.
2. Big Five Personality traits are linked to people’s tendency to prioritize rule adherence over being sympathetic towards individuals in daily moral dilemmas.
study_type Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
blinding No blinding is involved in this study.
study_design_overview In this study, participants will answer a collection of three surveys: (1) the Big Five personality questionnaire (i.e., Big Five Inventory -2 in the Expanded format), (2) a decision making tendency questionnaire consisted of 10 scenario-based questions, and (3) A short demographic questionnaire, which includes questions gender, age and ethnicity.

Once the data is collected, we will aggregate the scores on the personality questionnaire (by personality domains) and the behavioral tendency questionnaire. We then will compute the Pearson correlation coefficients between each personality domain score and people’s behaviral tendency scores as well as their associated p-values.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
data_collection_procedures We will collect convenient sample from a Canadian university. Participants will mostly be undergraduate students taking Psychology classes. Participants can voluntarily sign up for the study on a school-wise research participation platform, where they will be provided with the link to complete the questionnaire and a brief description of the study. Participants will first be met with the informed consent form, where their consent will be asked for prior to the start of the study. Participants will be informed that after giving consent they will be guaranteed their URPP credits, regardless of their completion or non-completion of the study. Once consent is collected, participants will then be prompted to complete (1) the Big Five personality questionnaire, (2) a decision making tendency questionnaire consisted of 10 scenario-based questions, and (3) A short demographic questionnaire.
sample_size Ideally, we hope to collect data from 200-300 participants, as this is the typical number used by studies on Personality and criteria variable prediction research.
stopping_rule The data collection process will end when one of the criteria is met:
1. We have collected 300 valid datapoints (excluding participants who signed up for but did not complete this study).
2. By the end of September, 2024, if we have 200 valid datapoints.
measured_variables Big Five Personality, as measured by Big Five Inventory -2 in Expanded format.
Decision Making Tendency: risk taking and empathetic tendency, as measured by 10 decision making scenarios.
Demographic variables: age, gender, ethnicity, and English Proficiency.
statistical_tests Once the data is collected, we will aggregate the scores on the personality questionnaire (by personality domains) and the behavioral tendency questionnaire. We then will compute the Pearson correlation coefficients between each personality domain score and people’s behaviral tendency scores as well as their associated p-values.
data_exclusion_criteria We will exclude datapoints from participants who are not proficient in English, because all the surveys are designed in English.
missing_data_handling If a participants does not complete all the questions on the personality or the decision making questionnaire, their data will not be included in the analysis.
